(Photo illustration using archival images.) It is the first time a UN climate summit has ended without a headline deal since Copenhagen in 2009 . COP31 was due to wrap up on Friday. Negotiators instead ran two days past the deadline, making it the longest UN climate summit on record and overtaking COP25 in Madrid in 2019, before Turkey's COP31 president, Murat Kurum, said there would be no further attempt at an agreement. Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the European Union in the closing plenary, said the EU and its member states formally objected to the "Antalya Pact" cover decision because "it fails to meet the moment." articles.description: Britain's Net Zero Revolution Has A China Problem Authored by City A.M. via OilPrice.com , The Labour government has been accused of "capitulation" in its trade relations with China as Britain's transition to net zero faces a number of security risks. A new report, published shortly before President Trump's momentous trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, has highlighted the UK's dependence on China for net zero-related technology and potential vulnerabilities in supply chains. Policy Exchange researchers found that China accounts for 91 percent of the UK's solar imports, plus 94 percent of permanent magnets used in wind power and around 70 percent of global battery production that is used in electric vehicles. articles.description: On Freedom In The Face Of Tyranny Authored by J.B. Shurk via American Thinker , As much as President Trump's supporters hoped that he would be able to save America from those who wish to destroy America, the midterm elections have made clear that this project will continue long after the president leaves office . Deep down, we knew this would be the case. The war for freedom is a war without end. It requires us to fight each and every day. For those who find the sound of that mission exhausting, remember that it is far less exhausting than the prospect of living in perpetuity under the yoke of totalitarianism . Here is the good news, if you are capable of receiving it as such: All you must do is never give up. That's it. Just rise each day with enough resolve in your heart to defend freedom against its enemies, and your persistence - nay, your refusal to surrender - combines invisibly with that of other Americans who share your commitment to press on despite inevitable setbacks, discouragements, and personal costs. articles.description: Former Postal Contractor Admits To Stealing Mail In Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Operation A Kansas City-area man who transported mail for the U.S. Postal Service has admitted to taking checks and financial cards from the mail system and supplying them to others involved in a fraud operation valued at more than $4.4 million, according to Fox 4 Kansas City . Michael D. McDowell, 42, pleaded guilty to federal offenses involving attempted bank fraud, aggravated identity theft, money laundering and possession of stolen mail. The U.S. Department of Justice estimates that the attempted losses connected to the stolen personal checks reached at least $4,466,000. Fox reports that the scheme unfolded while McDowell was employed by AiLO Logistics, a private transportation company providing delivery services under contract with USPS. Between October 2024 and May 2026, his duties included moving mail from a Kansas City processing facility to post offices in surrounding communities, including Grandview and Belton. articles.title: Taiwan Kills The Shorts: Blanket Ban, Stock-Lending Freeze And A $15 Billion Rescue Fund After The Taiex's Worst Week Since 1991
articles.description: Taiwan Kills The Shorts: Blanket Ban, Stock-Lending Freeze And A $15 Billion Rescue Fund After The Taiex's Worst Week Since 1991 Last Thursday we reported that " Taiwan Strangles The Shorts After The Taiex Loses 5,000 Points In Three Days ." Well, Taiwan has now killed them. On Saturday, one day after the Taiex wrapped up its worst week in 35 years , the island's Financial Supervisory Commission banned short selling below the previous day's closing price across the entire market, Bloomberg reported. The ban covers every listed and OTC stock, and it applies whether the shares are borrowed or shorted on margin. Separately, the Finance Ministry's NT$500 billion ($15 billion) National Financial Stabilization Fund confirmed that it is already in the market buying, and asked investors to keep the faith. The new rules kick in on Monday, November 23, and mark the third round of short-selling curbs in 15 days . The first two, as regular readers recall, did not go well. We ended Thursday's post by observing that with the short-sale quota already cut from 30% to 1%, there was "only one number left: zero." articles.description: Having been jailed for 10 years and six months, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand remains very much in the headlines. Since his conviction, six more women have come forward with allegations of misconduct. Meanwhile, Brand’s voice and image continue to be broadcast around the world, and not just in the form of news stories and documentaries. Brand’s X account remains open, and his popular YouTube channel recently uploaded a pre-recorded episode of his Sunday Service programme that also featured a post-sentencing letter penned by Brand and read aloud by his wife, Laura Gallacher. And the UK government is under pressure to change laws related to the age of sexual consent in the wake of Brand’s imprisonment. Fionnán Sheahan is joined by Daily Mail feature writer Fred Kelly and Irish Independent features journalist Kirsty Blake Knox to look at the impact that the jailing of Russell Brand has had on the disgraced comedian’s brand.

Customers may experience a loss of water supply or a drop in pressure when the work is being carried out. We are working to fix the problem as soon as possible. Discoloured water can occur when the mains are disturbed. This can happen when there has been an interruption to supply following a burst main and the operational activity associated with the repair. The discolouration will be short-lived, and running the tap for a while should help clear it from the system. All water is disinfected to ensure it is safe to drink. Following operational activity, the level of chlorine in the water supply may be boosted temporarily. The amount of chlorine is carefully controlled and monitored at our treatment works and strategic points in the distribution system. Water quality samples are taken following burst mains repairs to ensure that a satisfactory water supply is restored to customers If you need further help or advice, please contact us on 03457 440088 and one of our team will be here to help, 24 hours a day. articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed und

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?

Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. articles.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
articles.description: Hepworth Wakefield, West Yorkshire He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable. It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
articles.description: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. Continue reading...

articles.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
articles.description: After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’ The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter. In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity. Continue reading...

articles.title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days
articles.description: Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter. The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?
articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind. Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. Whatever your preferred publication, left or right, high- or lowbrow, it will have proffered its own take on the game, whether it’s to bemoan its godless influence on adolescent men or to laud its u

articles.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
articles.description: Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands. That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns ( lussekatter ) replaces cinnamon buns for fika , our revered tradition of coffee and cake. Continue reading...

articles.title: SNL’s skit Sister captures the quiet agony of caregiving for women: ‘I’ve never felt seen like that’
articles.description: The viral satirization of the caregiving burden left to women and daughters hit home for many viewers The Saturday Night Live sketch , titled Sister quickly went viral this week for its satirization of the burden that women and daughters face to take care of aging family members. In the parody commercial, comedian John Mulaney touts the benefit of “Sister”, who he describes as “a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister”. “Now I don’t have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do,” Mulaney says, as the sister, played by cast member Jane Wickline, gives their father’s medication to him. The sketch, which amassed over seven million views on YouTube in less than a week since it aired, has received thousands of responses and comments about its accuracy. “This is one of the MOST wicked and spot on SNL sketches ever written,” wrote one commenter on YouTube. Another posted: “As a hospice nurse this definitely tracks. I deal 90% of the time with adult daughters, and if there is no daughter, it is the daughter in law.” “This is so real it almost gav

articles.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
articles.description: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said. Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. articles.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
articles.description: Experts say BBLs and other cosmetic procedures can be risky and seasonal offers at clinics in England could make people rush decisions Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
articles.description: M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra. Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but

articles.title: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80
articles.description: Director and Scorsese collaborator is using AI in films and sees its takeover as inevitable, not just in cinema Paul Schrader was sipping white wine in a Greenwich Village trattoria when he said how he felt about using AI to make films: “I am opening the cage of a monster and I don’t have a leash.” The 80-year-old film-maker behind Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and American Gigolo, is embracing the technology as he enters the final act of a prolific career in which he has collaborated with Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro, Sigourney Weaver and Richard Gere. articles.title: Promise Me, America by Joe Biden review – former president defends his decisions
articles.description: New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party. Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election. Continue reading...

articles.title: Vienna on a plate: a food lover’s guide to the Austrian capital
articles.description: Some of the city’s best chefs, Ola Szwarc, Nadim Amin, Konstantin Filippou and Felix Mandl, share their favourite cafes, bars and restaurants There are two sides to coffee in Vienna. The grand, old-school coffee houses are incredible places to sit, have breakfast, drink a beer and forget about time. They have much the same function as a pub in Britain. For that experience, we’d go to Café Prückel or Café Hawelka . For a quintessential Viennese coffee, we’d suggest a wiener melange – somewhat similar to a cappuccino, but traditionally a little milder, made with coffee, steamed milk and milk foam. Alternatively, an einspänner is another peculiar, old-fashioned option: a strong black coffee served in a glass with a layer of cold whipped cream on top. If we want good coffee that actually wakes us up, we go to Kaffeemodul . You can choose the style you like, from fruity to less fruity. NA Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
articles.description: The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …” The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicke

articles.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . articles.title: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba

articles.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
articles.description: A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious I booked my lunch table at Cassette , a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple , mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell , the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27 , the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur. Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in her

articles.title: My husband has such bad breath we haven’t kissed in years – but he won’t see a dentist | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You clearly love him, but do you love yourself enough to stop letting him get away with this? I’ ve got a very upsetting problem in my marriage: my husband has extremely bad breath. We have been together for 20 years and it has always been noticeable, but has got worse in recent years. Recently, he lost a tooth, which he said he knocked out, but I’m pretty certain it fell out due to gum disease. I have spoken to him about this issue in the past, and even managed to get him to the dentist once, but he became so frightened that he ran out of the surgery. Since then, whenever I mention his breath or the dentist, he becomes very defensive. Continue reading...

articles.title: This is how we do it: ‘One time my son said: “I heard you having sex. It was disgusting.” That killed the vibe’
articles.description: Empty nesters Anna and Richard have found the freedom and space to experiment with intimacy • How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously I’m a much more active participant sexually now. I used to be more reactive Continue reading...

articles.title: The best thing I ever ate? Lunch on the strait of Hormuz
articles.description: The idea of any guest being hungry, or there not being enough food, is an unspeakable proposition for an Iranian host When most people think of the strait of Hormuz, the warm, tropical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, incredible food isn’t usually the first thing that comes to mind. But it should be, and I would know – it’s where I had one of my most memorable meals. I was visiting Iran, traversing thousands of miles across the country with a local female photographer, mapping out regional specialities for my cookbook The Saffron Tales . Over the course of several months, we cooked and ate in people’s home kitchens, meeting a cross-section of society, from farmers and pharmacists to yoga teachers and restaurant owners, who all shared their favourite foods with us in places as diverse as the snowy mountains outside Tabriz, the rice paddies of the Caspian Sea, and the historic cities of Isfahan and Shiraz. The Saffron Tales: Recipes and Stories from the Persian Kitchen by Yasmin Khan, published by Bloomsbury at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go to guardianbookshop.com Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Harsh to be under her thumb’: Pitchfork’s Ryan Schreiber on selling to Condé Nast and Anna Wintour
articles.description: He shocked the industry when he ‘sold out’ to corporate media in 2015. For the first time since leaving, he opens up about his new life as an out gay man and why he quit On the early November day that I met Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber in New York City, the website he created is all that anyone on my timeline can talk about, again. Today, it’s thanks to a freshly dug-up tweet from Jon Ossoff, the newly re-elected Georgia senator, who sincerely wrote in 2012: “Looking forward to your writeup of the new @imaginedragons album.” It’s an all-timer, up there with Phoebe Bridgers saying that she thinks about the site’s review of Jet’s second album (a video of a monkey pissing in its own mouth) once a day, and Halsey wishing that the Pitchfork office, which is on the site of the 9/11 attacks in New York, would “collapse already”. The joke in Ossoff’s case is that Pitchfork would not be caught dead praising the purveyors of stomp clap radio rock; a 2021 review characterized the band’s music as “emotions fired out of a T-shirt cannon”. Continue reading...

articles.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
articles.description: Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be. All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict . But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from

articles.title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
articles.description: Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London This truncated, candlelit version makes use of skilful percussion to occasionally fill in for oration but loses some of the play’s beauty and power Any modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company , which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison. This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
articles.description: The Texas singer was fascinated by Elvis Costello as a kid and admires Nancy Sinatra’s sass and strength, but which of her own songs changed her life? The first song I fell in love with My mum gave me an old Dansette record player and a pile of albums. I must have been eight or 10, with my younger sister Corinne, getting butterflies to These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra. Years later, I read that she was told to sing it with a much more provocative attitude. You can hear the sass and the strength. Maybe that’s where my whole “don’t fuck with me” thing came from. The song I do at karaoke Give me any Marvin Gaye song, like You’re All I Need to Get By, and I’m all over it, but I’d normally pull someone up to duet with me. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
articles.description: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats,

articles.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
articles.description: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the me

articles.title: Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow review – these audacious pranks are tell-your-friends funny
articles.description: Butler is a serious talent. These punchy, pacy shows see him taking on the establishment, industry by industry. He’s like a hipster Robin Hood It feels fitting that on the same weekend Nathan Fielder’s much-discussed You Can See Everything finally arrives in UK cinemas, Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow launches on the small screen. This wildly entertaining show confirms Butler as the British heir to Fielder’s crown as the clown prince of documentary-making. Butler doesn’t even need a gift-wrapped subject like Theranos grifter Elizabeth Holmes. If you enjoy satire that punches upwards at the rich and powerful, you’re in for a riotous treat. If you prefer a ghost-faced buffoon from Birmingham donning fancy dress to run rings around idiots, you’re also in luck. He might have a name like a valet-ordering app, but Oobah Butler is a serious talent. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
articles.description: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s
articles.description: Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped. The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
articles.description: Laura Brand says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday. This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults. Continue reading...

articles.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
articles.description: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found. Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rivals author Jilly Cooper accused of ‘extensive and deliberate plagiarism’
articles.description: Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists. The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey. Continue reading...

articles.title: US releases files on suspected Bigfoot sightings in Montana and Oregon
articles.description: Forest Service releases files months after residents in rural Ontario reported encounters with massive figures Bigfoot has quietly appeared again. Well, not Sasquatch directly, but new files about the cryptid. “The stride of the tracks did not change with slope.” “The tracks at both sites were not to the ‘bottom’ of the mud. “The small toes lack a definite ‘pad’ at the tips as would be expected.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable
articles.description: The summit’s failure was due to a refusal to admit we cannot confront the climate crisis without shifting to renewables The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned. “Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
articles.description: Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea. This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place. Continue reading...

articles.title: The footballer-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller
articles.description: Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich . The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace . In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “ Tolstoy enigma ”. Continue reading...

articles.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
articles.description: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? Con

articles.title: How to make nasi goreng – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
articles.description: The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time. Prep 25 min Chill 2 hr+ Cook 5 min Serves 2 Continue reading...

articles.title: Feeling the chill? Our favourite winter essentials on offer for Black Friday, from dehumidifiers to bedding
articles.description: From slow cookers and coats to dehumidifiers and lip balm, here’s everything you need to beat the big freeze for less – all recommended by the Filter UK • The best early Black Friday deals I love the idea of winter; every year I have idyllic visions of hunkering down under thick blankets and nursing a hot drink in front of a roaring fire. After suffering through this scorching summer, I have never been so delighted to feel a chill in the air. Unfortunately, cold weather rarely lives up to the fairytale in my head. The reality is often thermostat battles, dry skin, chapped lips, thick practical jackets covering cool outfits, and answering the door to the postman dressed in a shamefully crusty blanket hoodie. Continue reading...

articles.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
articles.description: ‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation. Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sorting through my mother-in-law’s belongings was heartbreaking. One generation’s treasure is the next’s trash | Emma Beddington
articles.description: Medals, ornaments, yellow-rimmed plates – so much life packed into binbags. What unwanted trinkets am I going to pass on? My mother-in-law recently moved from her apartment of several decades into sheltered housing and my husband and his brother were summoned to help. We arrived to find her arranging the last of 200-plus glasses on the table; the cupboards were still overflowing with oyster forks, tablecloths and, bafflingly, patchwork fabric artichokes. It went better than this threatened: after a whirlwind long weekend, we escaped with some crockery, a photograph of my husband as a cherubic spherical tot and “Queen Alexandra’s Christmas Gift Book 1908” (sepia snaps of scowling royals holding terriers). Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial
articles.description: Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country. Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorit

articles.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
articles.description: The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents. Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments . The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to  replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performa

articles.title: An age gap isn’t always a problem, partner abuse is | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to articles on relationships and the age of consent Regarding Polly Hudson’s article ( At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November ), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like. I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference. Continue reading...

articles.title: The link between nurturing and masculinity | Letter
articles.description: Clincal psychotherapist Gareth Strangemore-Jones responds to an article on persistent assumptions about masculinity Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature ( Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November ). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring. We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation. Continue reading...

articles.title: Let refugees work and contribute to our society | Letters
articles.description: Shirley Hart urges us to look beyond the labels of ‘asylum seeker’ and ‘refugee’ to see human beings forced to leave their homes. Plus a letter from Steve Wells Congratulations to Zoe Williams on her excellent article ( Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human?, 17 November ). I am the vice-chair of a charity in Hull that helps asylum seekers and refugees, and I have to say that the “service users” of Welcome House are some of the kindest, most polite and grateful people I have met. A young man who shared his gloves on a cold winter’s day so that he and his friend could have at least one warm hand. A young woman from Afghanistan who wants to have an education and qualify as a doctor. The group of young men who picked up 20 bags of litter to make Hull, a City of Sanctuary, a cleaner place to live. Continue reading...

articles.title: An album to keep your mind on track | Brief letters
articles.description: Steely Dan | Hot toddy | Dental advice | Christmas gifts | Black Friday I read with interest how Adrian Chiles traces his concentration challenges back to the CD shuffle button ( Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button, 18 November ). The simple solution is to play Aja by Steely Dan , in its glorious 39 minutes and 54 seconds’ entirety, and I promise you there will be absolutely no skipping or shuffling of tracks. Bren Pointer London • To mitigate the dental hygienist’s horror of a hot toddy ( Letters, 20 November ), how about having the hot water flavoured with sugar and lemon, followed by a swishing of the teeth with a generous helping of whisky? William Bryce Farnham, Surrey Continue reading...

articles.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
articles.description: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government. articles.title: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.description: District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights. JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices . Continue reading...

articles.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
articles.description: Utilita Arena Cardiff Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. Continue reading...

articles.title: Secrets, squabbles and laughs as a Jamaican family mourns in modern classic Nine Night
articles.description: Kiln theatre, London Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s tragicomedy about a matriarch’s wake is moving without a hint of mawkishness The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate). You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018 . Continue reading...

articles.title: Hark! Errollyn Wallen’s glittering nativity opera A Christmas Miracle is a credit to Britten’s community vision
articles.description: Orford church, Suffolk Performed in the venue where Noye’s Fludde premiered and based on the same text, this festive new work shines with exuberant young performers, distinctive singalongs, lustrous designs and the spirit of mucking in When Benjamin Britten wrote Noye’s Fludde, he essentially invented community opera. Bringing professionals together with enthusiastic local amateurs, everyone mucking in to play, sing and make sets and costumes, isn’t only great fun; done right, it fosters a love of music-making that can last a lifetime. Such projects, the composer declared with his best socialist hat on, created works that were “useful to the living”. For decades, Britten contemplated a nativity opera, which somehow never transpired. Now, Errollyn Wallen , Master of the King’s Music, has filled the gap. A Christmas Miracle, co-produced by Mahogany Opera and Britten Pears Arts, sets texts from the same Chester mystery plays that inspired Noye’s Fludde, and premiered in the Orford church that Britten chose in 1958. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tyson Fury looks back: ‘Once the Anthony Joshua fight is over, what will I do next? Walking the dog ain’t gonna cut it’
articles.description: The former heavyweight boxing champion on falling in love at first sight, being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and the much-anticipated match Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua . He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November. This was taken when I was nine, back when I was cute, shy and poorly dressed. The jumper would have been knitted by my grandma. The hairstyle isn’t great but a lot better than what I have now. I loved boxing and I loved singing. Continue reading...

articles.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stuck sitting in a sea of legs and feet when a beautiful young man offered me his hand
articles.description: This young man took the time to notice the middle-aged woman sitting in the dust and didn’t just walk past. He reached out Read more in the kindness of strangers series My knees aren’t in terribly good condition. I’m at that age. A few years ago, I was at a big hippy festival out in the Australian desert near Deniliquin. There, I attended a talk and was sitting down on the ground at the rear of a large group of people listening to a speaker. When the talk finished, everybody got up to leave, streaming past me as they went. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dining across the divide: ‘He feels the current wave of immigrants are less likely to assimilate’

articles.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
articles.description: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t. Continue reading...

articles.title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
articles.description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions ponders a quirk of the UK railway system • This week’s question: is there any way in which ‘manifesting’ can achieve the desired effect? I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com . When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest distance or any route no more than 3 miles longer, whether or not they pass through the common routeing point. Also permitted are journeys that use direct trains to and from the common routeing point. Continue reading...

articles.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
articles.description: For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad. For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
articles.description: Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks. Continue reading...

articles.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
articles.description: Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels. The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work. Continue reading...

articles.title: Peter Fluck obituary
articles.description: Artist and caricaturist who co-created the hugely popular ITV satire Sptting Image with Roger Law Peter Fluck, who has died aged 85, was, with his fellow artist Roger Law, half of the Fluck & Law partnership that revived satire on TV with Spitting Image, the ITV puppet sketch show lampooning celebrities, politicians and the royal family. Two decades after the BBC’s That Was the Week That Was spoofed the British establishment and, in particular, the last days of Harold Macmillan ’s Conservative government at the time of the John Profumo affair, Spitting Image, from 1984 to 1996, mined another period of Tory rule rich in distinctive characters, exaggerating elements of their personalities. Continue reading...

articles.title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
articles.description: Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal. Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
articles.description: Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned. Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
articles.description: Hayward Gallery, London The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching thems

articles.title: The Witch Farm review – this creepy tale is laugh-out-loud funny … without meaning to be
articles.description: Danny Robins follows up his Uncanny paranormal documentary about a Welsh farm with this drama. Subtle it isn’t – it’s bedlam from the get-go and at times it’s so OTT it’s unwittingly hilarious A lot of strange and scary stuff happened in 1989 at Heol Fanog, a lonely farmhouse at the foot of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly known as the Brecon Beacons). English artist Bill Rich and his pregnant Welsh partner, Liz, moved there with Bill’s teenage son to begin again, replacing the complexity of urban life with the still silence of the remote countryside. But their new start became a protracted nightmare when they experienced what seemed to be supernatural phenomena – and the Heol Fanog ghosts would keep appearing to the Rich family for another seven years. The case – nicknamed the “Welsh Amityville” for its similarities to the US’s most famous instance of reported paranormal activity – has long haunted Danny Robins, presenter of the podcast and BBC Two TV series Uncanny, in which he investigates claims of interactions with the undead. Heol Fanog stands out because of the sheer number of eerie events, the length of time across which they took place, and the multiple witnesses: if you can e

articles.title: Gerwyn Price ends barren run with Grand Slam of Darts win: ‘Now they can stop talking’
articles.description: Price beats Gian van Veen 16-11 to secure title Welshman lost ‘so many finals’ in four years of pain Gerwyn Price finally ended his major trophy drought by winning the Grand Slam of Darts and is delighted to silence his critics. The Welshman had not won a major televised event since 2022 and may have thought it might not happen again after losing three finals this year alone. But with Luke Littler and Luke Humphries exiting early, Price took his chance with a brilliant 16-11 win over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton. Price claimed Grand Slam glory for the fourth time, but this one will surely mean the most to him. Continue reading...

articles.title: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer
articles.description: Harlequins 21-48 Bristol Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope and she was dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her Bristol debut. The full-back did it under significant pressure too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener. The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old, and if her debut is anything to go by he will be proved right. The World Cup winner not only scored two tries but was also a linchpin in Bristol’s attack. Her gamechanging reputation was felt among her former teammates as she drew multiple defenders to her whenever she had the ball, meaning the wings on her outside had a lot more joy. The back three looked formidable with both wings

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’
articles.description: Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage. “If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.” Continue reading...

articles.title: At least 24 killed and dozens missing in confectionery factory fire in Indonesia

Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. articles.title: ‘A Nintendo Switch – yes, I know I’m 67’: the best gifts for every generation, picked by real people aged 2 to 103
articles.description: We asked everyone from gen Alpha preschoolers to retired boomers, celebs and Guardian writers what’s on their gift list this year – here’s what they said • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 How old are you, and what would you like for Christmas? That’s normally a question reserved for children visiting Santa’s grotto, but it’s one we put to hundreds of you of all ages to see what different generations have on their gift lists. The results may just help you hone your approach to present buying across generations this Christmas, or at least offer an insight into the tastes of each group. But be warned: from the boomer who wants a Nintendo Switch to the 30-somethings collecting vinyl and brewing craft beer, some answers might surprise you. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
articles.description: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
articles.description: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with colla

articles.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
articles.description: While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip. The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales. Continue reading...

articles.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
articles.description: Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave. To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce. Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre Continue reading...

articles.title: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
articles.description: Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically. This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event. Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’ Continue reading...

articles.title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
articles.description: Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’ Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report. Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come. Continue reading...

articles.title: Manchester’s Co-op Live arena evacuated after ‘unknown substance’ released in crowd
