Police declared a major incident after the release of the substance, which was initially thought to be teargas, as they sought to protect the 12,000 people in the crowd at a Don Toliver concert. Continue reading...

articles.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
articles.description: Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency. Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
articles.description: Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants. Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Burnham not ‘backtracking’ on creating closer links with EU, officials say

articles.title: Fewer than half in UK will pay TV licence fee within a decade, report warns
articles.description: Analysis for thinktank points to cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on content in ‘spiral of decline’ Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline” . With senior BBC figures concerned about the accelerating fall in licence fee sales, the independent projections also warn that the proportion of households paying the levy will further decline to less than a third by 2037-38 should the government persist with the corporation’s current funding model. articles.title: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31

Here are six key takeaways from Cop31. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the f-word failure is not his alone

Continue reading...

articles.title: Apple iPhone Duo review: the most novel and interesting iPhone in almost a decade
articles.description: The folding iPhone is early-adopter gold, changing the way iOS works and successfully condensing a tablet into your pocket, but it is not for everyone Apple’s first folding phone has upended the usual order of things with some interesting choices about how you use a iPhone – for better or worse. The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined. articles.title: Drivers trapped in limbo due to DVLA licence delays
articles.description: It had been revoked on medical grounds but after 12 months I was invited to restore it. Nine months later my application was untouched My driving licence was revoked on medical grounds after I underwent brain surgery for a vascular lesion in 2024. After waiting the required 12 months for my health to stabilise, I was invited to apply for my licence to be restored. I duly sent the evidence from hospital consultants and medical tests. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
articles.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. Continue reading...

articles.title: Can you solve it? How Super Mario explains Renaissance art
articles.description: A step or a jump Today’s puzzle is about the hidden mathematical pattern behind a much-loved video game. Consider a simplified game of Super Mario. He moves from platform to platform. He can either step forward 1 space, to the next platform, or jump forward 2 spaces, to the platform after that. 3 platforms? 4 platforms? 5 platforms? 10 platforms? Continue reading...

articles.title: David Byrne on the great ideas that got away | Today in Focus
articles.description: David Byrne has had more than a lifetime’s worth of genius ideas. The kind that influence art and music decades after they first came about. As the frontman of Talking Heads, Byrne has made some of the greatest albums of all time. He tells Nosheen Iqbal about his new book, Sleeping Beauties , in which he explores why so many breakthroughs in science, economics and culture were lost on their initial audience and only later revived and acknowledged to be great. He writes: 'Our view of ourselves and the world changes, not always in a linear manner, and what was once forgotten can be reawakened and can come to seem obvious and valuable' Continue reading...

articles.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
articles.description: Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives. There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell. Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the

articles.title: Nasa, please send me to the moon. Science says I’m the perfect crew member | Helen Pilcher
articles.description: Women of my age have been training for this job for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. articles.title: Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle
articles.description: Footage of Saturday incident, filmed by fellow passengers, quickly went viral on social media as mayor calls tactics ‘un-American’ Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge as they boarded their Alaska Airlines flight. articles.title: Grieving families getting into debt and doing without memorials due to benefit freezes

Today, that is a pipe dream,” said Lindesay Mace, a co-manager of Down to Earth, a funeral costs support service run by the charity Quaker Social Action. Continue reading...

articles.title: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns
articles.description: Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa , saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder. “To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain
articles.description: Encouraged by his grandfather and single mother, the teen Borja dreams of a career that will end his family’s poverty, but the protesters are gathering strength Where last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida . Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja. Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. Everything in his vicinity seems to point in the direction of the bullring: the Playmobil corrida he stages with his little brother, Erik, the mechanical rodeo bulls they ride at the fairground, the lessons in handling the muleta – the red cloth – he gets from grandfather, Matias, whose own bullfighting ambitions were scotched at an early age. But, as the protesters piling into the arena one day highlig

articles.title: TV tonight: inside the disturbing plot to murder Holly Willoughby
articles.description: The full horror of Gavin Plumb’s abduction fantasy revealed. Plus: a privileged glimpse inside the Doge’s Palace with Lucy Worsley. Here’s what to watch this evening 9pm, Channel 4 This deeply disturbing film enters the world of stalking and abduction chatgroups to explore the 2023 plot to kidnap, rape and murder Holly Willoughby. Fortunately, Gavin Plumb did his planning with a man he knew as “David Nelson” – who turned out to be an undercover American cop. The film explores the foiled plot and also examines the opportunities the authorities missed to arrest Plumb for prior offences. Phil Harrison Continue reading...

articles.title: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
articles.description: The Hollywood star is joined by celebrity guests as she shares ‘practical tips’. Plus, David Cameron’s deeply personal series about Alzheimer’s The second podcast from her wellness empire is ostensibly centred on Paltrow’s incredibly niche lifestyle advice: where to eat the “best cacio e pepe in Rome”, for example, or “whether it’s weird to use an obsidian gua sha tool on a plane”. In reality, the show is a weekly cosy chat with a showbiz pal (first up, Zoe Saldaña) peppered with a few practical tips – such as how to eat enough protein if you can’t face any more eggs. Rachel Aroesti Widely available, episodes weekly Continue reading...

articles.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
articles.description: Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me! Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Top deck of the bus for the finest views of autumn | John Gilbey
articles.description: Cadair Idris, Gwynedd: Past golden hillsides and the great Cadair Idris, through wooded valleys, to the starting point for my walk The morning starts bright but cold, with a hazy mist clinging to the trees across the valley. This could be one of the last good weather days, so I take the bus north into Gwynedd, clambering awkwardly upstairs to get the best view of the autumn colours. The mist begins to clear and, in a wet meadow, a heron stands alertly by a ditch, watching for movement. Beyond the Afon Dyfi, the hills are golden with patches of larch and the deeper orange tones of the oak and ash. Well-defined shadows below the dark blue sky shelter pockets of still-frosted gloom, as we cross the Dyfi into Gwynedd. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pochettino’s new-manager bounce falls flat with De Ligt move a disastrous step | Jamie Jackson
articles.description: Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino. This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars
articles.description: After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says “I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
articles.description: Leeds offer Chelsea a lesson, Newcastle’s summer recruits struggle and Jules Ahoka makes a name for himself What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. Leny Yoro’s very early red card may have been questionable but for the wall to evaporate and allow Dominik Szoboszlai’s subsequent free-kick to arrow home was damning evidence of how immature Pochettino’s new charges are. From here it became a debacle and the players, if they have anything about them, need to apologise to the head coach, hold a meeting between themselves and demand they start taking responsibility. If not, United are heading only one way: down. Jamie Jackson Match report: Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United ‘It’s painful for me’: Pochettino criticises Yoro red card decision Continue reading...

articles.title: England and Ireland provide champagne rugby for north to tee up finals weekend | Robert Kitson
articles.description: France have the chance to topple the Springboks in the Nations Championship decider, with their Six Nations rivals also shining this autumn Even if the official November Test window had now closed, as used to be the case, this would already have been a vintage European autumn. Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday. Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka. A r ecord-breaking 37-12 home win was then swiftly followed by Ireland defeating the world champion Springboks 20-17 to complete another resounding northern hemisphere double whammy. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Ravens have long been a model of stability. Now they’re going off the rails
articles.description: Baltimore have been one of the most successful teams in the league this century. But recent events have dinged their reputation The Baltimore Ravens have lost in all sorts of fashion in recent weeks. There were the blowout losses to juggernauts Buffalo, Jacksonville, and Cincinnati. There was the nailbiting divisional loss to Cleveland. There was the embarrassing defeat to the previously winless Chargers. But Sunday’s 35-33 loss to Carolina , the team’s sixth straight, hit different. Sunday was a massive test. Did Baltimore have the fortitude to bounce back and stay alive in the AFC North, with the hope of getting the injured Lamar Jackson back at some point? Almost. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gukesh vows to win world chess title ‘all over again’ as Sindarov challenge looms
articles.description: Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday Uzbek challenger enters as the oddsmakers’ favorite Champion plays down slump after falling to No 26 Read our World Chess Championship watch guide World chess champion Gukesh Dommaraju insisted he was approaching his first title defense with the mindset of a challenger on Sunday as he and Javokhir Sindarov faced the media ahead of their historic showdown in Geneva, the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. The two 20-year-old grandmasters appeared side by side at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva, where they struck a respectful tone before their best-of-14-games encounter begins on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Haaland must be worried’: Thierno Barry’s rise has David Moyes purring
articles.description: Everton striker has worked hard to find his scoring touch after admitting he hit ‘rock bottom’ at times last season A most unexpected name sits behind the phenomenon Erling Haaland and the £125m proven marksman Alexander Isak in the Premier League goalscoring chart this season. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the refusal to quit. “Fabulous” was David Moyes’s take on Barry’s last performance for Everton, when a double against Coventry took the striker to 10 goals for the season in all competitions and his team temporarily up to fifth. It was high praise indeed from a manager who does not dispense tributes freely, and can appear to be on the French forward’s case constantly, but was no more than Barry deserved for a display that also featured an assist for Everton’s third goal of the night. His six Premier League goals leave him joint third alongside Evanilson of Bournemouth and Aston Villa’s Nicolas Jackson. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
articles.description: Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves Business live – latest updates European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills. The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks– rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
articles.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: ‘Music was our teacher’: the sound system pioneers reviving the scene in Manchester and beyond
articles.description: Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the history lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms, but through towering stacks of amps and speakers, turntables and Jamaican records. “We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley, Culture, that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. For us, the sound system was not just entertainment – it was an education.” Continue reading...

articles.title: McBurnie’s added-time double snatches win for Hull to shock 10-man Brighton
articles.description: Amid the talk of Brighton being surprise title contenders this season, these are perhaps the afternoons which show the margin that still exists, and how the Premier League can provide the most punishing of wake-up calls at any moment. Make no mistake about it, Fabian Hürzeler’s side will play far worse than this over the next few months and win. They are still second in the table. How they left Hull without even a point almost defies belief given the dominance they enjoyed for large parts of the contest. But for all the statement victories and the headline-grabbing moments , these games are the ones which can trip you up the most. Continue reading...

articles.title: Max Verstappen says George Russell is ‘so far below my level’ after Vegas win
articles.description: Red Bull driver delighted rival crashed out of grand prix Leclerc and Hamilton relationship is ‘unmanageable’ Max Verstappen escalated his feud with George Russell after a stunning victory at the Las Vegas Grand Prix , stating the British driver was barely worth consideration because he was “so far below my level”. The Dutchman competed with Russell for much of the race in Nevada but it was the Red Bull driver who came out on top and Russell ultimately fell to ninth after he suffered a lock-up late in the race. Continue reading...

articles.title: Manchester City’s WSL title bid hit by Spurs after Vinberg and Naz’s late double
articles.description: This most unpredictable and evenly contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive defeat, by virtue of a terrific performance from a Tottenham side who moved within three points of the European places. The shock result came just 24 hours after City’s title rivals Chelsea had dropped points at Liverpool. It was the first time City had failed to win a home league match during Andrée Jeglertz’s 16 months in charge, let alone lose. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s painful for me’: Pochettino criticises Yoro red card in Anfield humiliation
articles.description: Manchester United lose 4-0 to Liverpool after early red Argentinian suffers club’s joint-heaviest debut defeat Mauricio Pochettino argued that Leny Yoro was wrongly sent off and that Manchester United were earlier denied a penalty against Liverpool after suffering the joint-heaviest debut defeat in the club’s history. Liverpool’s emphatic 4-0 win ensured Pochettino equalled Lal Hilditch’s unwanted record from 1926 of losing his first United game by such a scoreline. United’s 34 goals conceded across all competitions this season are the most by any team in European football’s top five leagues. Continue reading...

articles.title: Alcaraz puts Zverev in shade as world’s best beats No 1 for first ATP Finals title
articles.description: Spaniard wins final 6-2, 7-6 (7) against new world No 1 Alcaraz the fourth to win career grand slam and ATP Finals The titles of ATP world No 1 and the best male tennis player in the world are carried by two different names. This has always been clear throughout this messy, injury-ravaged men’s season but it was underlined in the grand finale as Carlos Alcaraz ended his campaign with a statement victory, defeating the top-ranked player, Alexander Zverev, 6-2, 7-6 (7) to win the ATP Finals for the first time. So much of Alcaraz’s fortunes this season were defined by the wrist injury that forced him out for four and a half months during the spring and summer. No matter, he still managed to tick the two most important items off his to-do list this year. Continue reading...

articles.title: Steve Borthwick hits rewind button to inspire England’s flying starts
articles.description: The head coach said he has watched videos from Eddie Jones’ time in charge to help England begin matches strongly Ellis Genge was so fired up by England’s powerful response to the haka on Saturday he stripped off his anthem jacket in the aftermath, completely forgetting he was not starting. Ollie Chessum told Lewis Moody, who had been invited to stand at the point of England’s V formation: “We are going long left, stay on the field and chase the kick-off.” And according to Ben Earl, who would still be out on the Twickenham turf carrying through traffic if he could, some players were so inspired by Moody’s speech the night before they could not sleep. Against that emotional backdrop, it is small wonder England flew out of the blocks against the All Blacks . Steve Borthwick has spoken a lot about “bringing the fire” recently and on Saturday they torched the place, riding the emotional wave that Moody’s presence inspired from Henry Slade’s fourth-minute try, through to a record victory against New Zealand . Continue reading...

Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added. Continue reading...

The announcement, just after Wall Street closed for the week, saw Oracle describe itself as the first hyperscaler fully funded for the current artificial intelligence investment cycle. Over the weekend Oracle posted on social media that it had secured full financing for its contracts with OpenAI. This is a $300bn arrangement whereby Oracle would finance a 5-year cloud computing arrangement for the maker of ChatGPT. This would provide large scale AI infrastructure and compute capacity to power OpenAI. Oracle then confirmed that it would post positive free cash flow in fiscal 2028. This did not reassure all of the market, with some AI critics seizing on this statement as a sign that the lady doth protest too much, and Oracle must be in trouble. Some analysts are now convinced that Oracle relies on Nvidia to backstop this arrangement, and the risk is that without Jensen Huang at the helm, the deal could fall through. articles.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Less than 1% of Americans serve in the military. articles.title: Sanders, Slotkin say they won’t back Schumer for majority leader
articles.description: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) announced Tuesday that they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in his effort to become majority leader next year. The duo — leading voices on the center and left of the Democratic Party — took pains to avoid discussing specific policy issues, arguing instead that it is time for a new generation of leaders to take charge. "If this campaign was about anything, it was about change," Sanders said, adding that “poll after poll suggests that the American people want bold change.” “The public is done with people who say a lot of words but aren’t actually going to put more money in people’s pockets,” Slotkin said. “I personally will work with anyone who wants to work on that mission instead of looking like we’re doing things.” Neither Sanders nor Slotkin specified who they would support in the race for majority leader, though Slotkin said she had a “productive conversation” with Sen. articles.title: Are Democrats ready to make the most of the blue wave?
articles.description: Unless you’ve been living under a rock (no shame Patrick Star!), you’ve likely heard about last Tuesday’s “Blue Wave” midterm elections . The Democrats’ strong performance at the polls flipped control of the House and the Senate, delivering stunning results on the way, including flipping long-time red states like Kansas and Texas. As the GOP scrambles to repair the damage and Democrats strategize about how to use their new power in a divided Washington, one takeaway seems obvious: this was a foreign policy election, in which the Iran war and the costs it brought home served as the tipping point. But can we read these election results as a repudiation of U.S. foreign policy writ-large, or is this a specific response to one of the dumbest interventions in the long history of American adventurism? What does JD Vance's day-after effort to distance himself from the war tell us about how Republicans are digesting this result? And if Tuesday was a rebuke of U.S. foreign policy as usual, are Democrats ready to respond accordingly? articles.description: The Best Is Yet To Come Undone Submitted by QTR's Fringe Finance Today’s column is going to be two parts. First, I’m going to review a lot of what I’ve written about on this blog the last two weeks. Punk band Lit had a great song called “The Best Is Yet To Come (Undone).” After Friday’s market crash and headlines suggesting that the SEC could be investigating Nvidia’s accounting, I can’t think of a more appropriate title for my column this weekend. articles.description: Jeffrey Tucker: The Great Measles Scare, And Post-Pandemic Germophobia Authored by Jeffrey A. Tucker via The Epoch Times , The period following a pandemic has usually been marked by a cultural germophobia. It's an irrational fear of infection. The tendency is to treat the air as dirty, people as disease vectors, and have inordinate fear of any sign of sickness. People are also more susceptible to believing any quack selling a potion as a preventive. This happened after 1918. The cultural panic over germs and infections did not stop for a generation. I'm not sure if the measles frenzy out there in the media now is sticking in the population, but the volume has become unbearably intense. Did you know that we had a measles elimination status? Maybe I did; I don't remember. articles.description: Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit Cop31 live – latest updates The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster. articles.title: ‘The platonic ideal of a wine glass’: we test the best for every budget
articles.description: Searching for a wine glass that can do it all? From short-stemmed to swirlable, dishwasher-friendly to delicate, here’s the glassware that’s a cut above the rest • The best no- and low-alcohol wines for when you’re off the booze It is a truth only sometimes acknowledged that wine is in want of a good drinking vessel. Why? Because wine experts agree that the shape, character and feel of a glass give wine the conditions to shine. “A good glass can greatly improve your experience,” writes David Williams in The Encyclopedia of Wine . He adds that expense isn’t necessary: “[A]s a rule, the thinner the glass the better, while an oval shape and generous (but not enormous) bowl are best at capturing and releasing a wine’s flavours.” Drinking wine is an experience beyond flavour; before the taste, there is the nose, and a good glass will amplify its aromas. Likewise, there is the ineffable question of how a wine makes us feel; again, your choice of glass feeds into this experience – how does it feel to hold, to swirl, to sip from? Continue reading...

Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests and beaches. articles.title: A Robbie Williams film starring a CGI chimp helped me come to terms with my hearing loss
articles.description: I was bullied for my deafness as a child, and just when I was finding myself, a car crash set me back years. But then I watched the movie Better Man, and had my life explained for me I cannot say I’ve ever been a Robbie Williams fan. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life. I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. I was a misfit in my family, with no support for my deafness, and at school the bullying – from kids and teachers – was something awful. In my desperate isolation, I turned to reading: book reading, lip-reading, and reading the room. Forget TV, forget music – the Beano and Beezer were my survival manuals: the Numskulls taught me how my brain worked with broken ears. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Napping together on the reeds, the swans appeared luminous’: Noah Forster’s best phone picture
articles.description: The photographer hopes his intimate photograph of two sleeping birds will remind others of their special person Twenty-one-year-old Noah Forster had always thought swans were beautiful, but it was his girlfriend Cecilia is the one who made him really notice them. The pair began dating two years ago, but now live 70 miles apart; he is a welder in Newark-on-Trent, she is studying law in Leeds. “The distance can be difficult, but we try to talk as much as possible,” Forster says. “It’s taken me a while to save up for a driver’s licence and car, so I have a daily walk from my home and across the River Trent to get the 6am train to work. We like to send photos of our day to each other, and I took this photo on an exceptionally cold and frosty morning in November, walking across the river to get to work. I saw these swans near the castle. Napping together on the reeds, they appeared luminous.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’
articles.description: There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles. Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. articles.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
articles.description: I believe human judgment remains essential Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics? In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned. Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions. articles.description: As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK Britain is confronting its cult problem. articles.title: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.description: What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph. Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. articles.title: Bill’s Included review – Rob Brydon’s new character is as glorious as Gavin & Stacey’s Uncle Bryn
articles.description: The comic is sublime as a middle-aged landlord attempting to befriend student tenants. It’s very sweet – but the storylines and supporting characters are flimsy to say the least Bill Beam (Rob Brydon) is a chump, a sap, a bejumpered limpet clinging to the peripheries of his own existence. “I’m being left behind,” he tells best friend Drew (Kevin Eldon) who, having heard this – and that, and the other – a thousand times before, stifles a well-earned yawn. Bill’s wife has left him for the gardener (“No hard feelings!”) and lo, this ever-dimming bulb of cable-knit neediness must find a solution to both his newfound “cashflow crisis” and deepening existential haplessness. What to do? Enter, stage left, a fire at the local student halls and, with it, an answer to the plonker’s prayers: Bill will rent out his spare bedrooms to four undergraduates. Yes! This will provide him with the requisite dosh, a much-needed sense of purpose and a fresh audience for his piping-hot takes on Jeremy Beadle, the big Asda and the fact that his phone number is “one of only nine UK landlines to conclude with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4.” Go tell it on the mountain! But bring a sad trombone while you’re at it. Bec

articles.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
articles.description: For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful? • This article does not contain major spoilers Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there . Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding. articles.title: Chinese Researchers Develop Electronic Comb That Achieves Nearly 98% Hair Regrowth In Mice
articles.description: Chinese Researchers Develop Electronic Comb That Achieves Nearly 98% Hair Regrowth In Mice Researchers from Beihang University and City University of Hong Kong have developed an innovative electronic comb that could offer a promising new solution for treating hair loss, according to the South China Morning Post.  Called Detangle, the device combines electrical stimulation with advanced drug-delivery technology. During normal combing, it generates controlled electrical pulses that temporarily increase the permeability of hair follicle cells, allowing therapeutic compounds to penetrate deeper into the scalp. The comb features specially designed teeth equipped with microelectronic components and medication-release mechanisms. This system delivers two therapeutic agents simultaneously: one promotes blood vessel formation around hair follicles, while the other helps block hormonal processes associated with hair loss. In a 28-day experiment involving mice, the device achieved an impressive 97.85% hair regrowth when electrical stimulation was combined with medication every three days. articles.title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
articles.description: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. articles.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
articles.description: Isaac Eiger’s solo venture leaves jangle pop behind for a wilder sound. Often it owes a debt to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days? From New York via Montana Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children). Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. As always, my wife takes command of the situation In the year since my father-in-law died my wife and I have visited his cottage, on average, every other week – more often in spring and summer. In theory, this is often enough to keep abreast of appointments with people coming to deal with various issues: slipped roof slates, fallen trees, electrical problems. In practice, more can go wrong than gets put right in the interval. This time we’ve been away for three weeks. My son was meant to go down, but his plans changed. I’m dark, gothic Maga.” On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940. For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 35 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size. articles.title: César Azpilicueta: ‘At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe – if you can’t perform, you’re out’
articles.description: Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot. It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. The findings show that Walmart was identified as the lowest-priced major grocery chain in just five states , while competitors Aldi, Lidl and WinCo dominated the rankings. The analysis, which relayed on Consumer Reports pricing data and grocery chain locations, identified the lowest-priced major supermarket chain included in the comparison operating in each state. Aldi emerged as the runaway winner, taking the top spot in 32 states , including California, Florida, Texas, Ohio and Illinois. German discount rival Lidl claimed eight states, including New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia. Employee-owned WinCo took the crown in five western states, while Walmart managed to finish first only in Alaska, Colorado, Hawaii, New Mexico and Wyoming. The price differences were significant. articles.description: Buy And Forget? It's Not That Easy Authored by Michael Lebowitz via RealInvestmentAdvice.com , Buy an S&P 500 index fund, set up automatic contributions, and forget about it. It's one of the most common pieces of retirement advice, and the chart below makes a strong case for it. In January 1940, the S&P 500, as reconstructed by Robert Shiller, stood at about 12. Today, it's around 7,500. World War II, regional wars, recessions, oil shocks, a pandemic, and a long list of financial crises look like minor speed bumps. For anyone saving for retirement, the answer seems obvious: why do anything other than buy and forget? Unfortunately, it's not that easy.   The chart shows what the market did over 86 years.  It doesn't show what happened to investors who depended on it during the 20 or 30 years that mattered most to them. "The Best Laid Plans Of Mice And Men Often Go Awry" To illustrate why, consider a hypothetical example. A hypothetical investor born in 1940 starts to save for retirement in 1965 at age 25. articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
articles.description: (CDR) Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion. Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. articles.title: Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?
articles.description: Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world . On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg). People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
articles.description: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than incr

articles.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
articles.description: A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026 , but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck ’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it , even given their extravagant headgear. A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. articles.title: We should be free to call ourselves Black English | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article about categories on the census form It’s about time we fixed the Black English category in the census, whether popular or not ( It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose, 14 November ). Categories count. They make citizens, politically engineer belonging and allow people to be seen and to see themselves. The excuse that the Black English category is simply unpopular doesn’t wash. I remember in the 1990s when the Black British, or Black African categories were all the rage, they were never particularly comfortable to tick, but we all got over ourselves and stomached the flattening of our complex identities for what we believed was a good cause. A Black English category would also help me out enormously, living as I do in France, where people don’t believe me when I say I’m English, but simply think I’m deluded and can’t speak French properly – which I can. Having left Scotland when I was three and grown up in London, I felt I couldn’t legitimately call myself Scottish – but English, I could. articles.title: Judges, juries and rape myths in trials | Letters
articles.description: Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham In your report ( ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November ), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind. It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters
articles.description: Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas Rachel Dixon’s article ( The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November ) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around  £1,000 a year , and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten. It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters
articles.description: Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter “Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments ( Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November ). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation. It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told that “it’s fine”, but as a long-Covid sufferer for 2.5 years, I can tell you this disease is vile: I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy, certainly not my loved ones. I am unable to go for a walk, be social or stay active. If people feel ill (even “just a cold”) they should stay at home and avoid spreading their germs to everyone they meet, because they probably won’t know who is vulnerable. Sally Billenness Hounslow, London

articles.title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash
articles.description: Young Vic, London Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama. Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
articles.description: The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway; Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron; Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel; The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson; The Bells of Fortune by Leonora Nattrass The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22) The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People. The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. articles.title: Northern Ballet’s Cinderella spices the fairytale with festive fun and a sweet twist
articles.description: Norwich Theatre Royal Magic is sprinkled over Michael Pink’s elegant show, with the spirited score played by the Northern Ballet Sinfonia It wouldn’t be the first time an ugly sister has stolen the show. Andrew Tomlinson is a hoot in Northern Ballet’s new Cinderella as a klutzy, vainglorious stepsister with a great line in lovably grotesque facial expressions. He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet. Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. articles.description: The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.” Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic. That combination of richness, lightness, and the pure, sensual pleasure of it melting gently across the palate maintains an unbreakable hold over my imagination. In fact, other than fruit, it’s the only sweet food with which I have a genuine emotional relationship: I can remember many ice-creams I’ve eaten incredibly vividly, and in a way I just don’t with almost all other desserts and pastries. Today’s ice is a case in point, having been developed from a memory of an almond gelato eaten in Sicily just after the annual harvest. articles.title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall
articles.description: Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider ( Araneus diadematus ) outside our back window. Is that a smile? Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived nearby. Contemporary experiments with honeybees have shown that diversity in workers’ personality traits makes for an adaptable and resilient hive. Continue reading...

Full of chef bravado, I promised the father that I’d make him the best bowl of breakfast porridge he’d ever had. He, of course, turned up his nose at my bowl of sweet dessert, which I’d laced with cream and sugar, and showed me how to make porridge with just water and salt instead. I’ve never looked back. In my experience, most jumbo oats need twice as much water as the packet instructions suggest, as well as three times as long to cook and turn satisfyingly creamy. articles.title: What do I want from Santa? No more lazy, joyless Christmas lists | Polly Hudson
articles.description: Yes, life is simpler when you know precisely what your friends and family want to find under the tree. But bang goes any chance to surprise them – or show that you really care If the first step is admitting there’s a problem, please consider this an intervention. Many of us need help, and what I’m suggesting is pretty much a cold turkey approach, no pun intended. The Christmas list must be abolished, once and for all. It’s tricky to remember when it started, but, in my experience at least, this way of festive gifting has ramped up over the past few years, and is now threatening to become the norm. And it makes sense. Modern life is exhausting, and hard, so of course we leap gratefully onboard with anything that promises to make it easier. If a list is sent, or simply a direct link to one product, we can achieve with a few thumb movements from the comfort of the sofa what used to necessitate a journey, a fight through crowds, some searching, some queueing, and then a return journey. Instead, now, a couple of taps and a swipe, job done, lemon squeezy. But we’re not noticing what’s getting lost. On the surface we are all being given exactly what we want, but are we really? articles.description: "Now We Have The Answer": Retrial Jury Convicts Man Who Sparked Palisades Inferno Authored by Beige Luciano-Adams via The Epoch Times , LOS ANGELES - After deliberating for less than two days, a Los Angeles jury unanimously found a federal arson suspect guilty of lighting a brush fire in the Santa Monica Mountains that would lead, days later, to the catastrophic Palisades Fire of 2025 . The retrial of Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, began Nov. 4 after jurors in a first trial deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal in June , leading U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang to declare a mistrial . Rinderknecht, a dual U.S.-French citizen, pleaded not guilty to a revised indictment charging him with two counts of federal arson related to damage to federal property and property used in interstate commerce. The jury on Nov. 20 found him guilty on both counts. Sentencing in the case is set for March 17, 2027. The charges carry a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and a combined statutory maximum of 40 years. Investigators alleged that the defendant on Jan. 1 ignited a brush fire, dubbed the Lachman Fire, which smoldered underground for a week until reemerging to the surface through a single shrub.

articles.description: San Francisco Streets Flood With Sewage As Infrastructure Fails Liberals often fancy themselves the societal fount of art and creative culture.  It this is the case, then it is also fair to say that they are absolutely terrible at administration, maintenance and leadership.  Artists and bohemians should stick to cultural expression and stay out of the business of running cities or countries. San Francisco is a perfect example of this problem. Recent storms have overwhelmed San Francisco’s combined sewer system, causing widespread flooding and sewage backups which are wreaking havoc on business districts.  Even worse, “geysers” are exploding from manholes in multiple neighborhoods, tinged with what locals call "poop water". Many officials blame historic rainfall. The city has received roughly 2.5 inches of rain in a single day (with some reports of an average near 3 inches citywide), more than a typical full November’s rainfall.
