articles.title: I’m engaged but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel? | Leading questions
articles.description: Telling him would risk a lot of harm, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. If you’re going to take that gamble, you’d better be sure why you’re doing it Read more Leading questions My partner and I are engaged after a whirlwind romance, and I was over the moon when he proposed. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings. Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships
articles.description: Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change . I have spoken to people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s, describing age gaps far greater than three years; often with people twice their age or more. It’s noticeable that social norms and taboos didn’t change hugely between the start of the 1960s and the end of the 80s; in most cases, their pare

articles.title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples
articles.description: We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us • The best early Black Friday deals Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. articles.title: The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same | Gordon Brown
articles.description: As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France , Poland , Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism. Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states . Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east , Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south. articles.title: Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City | Imogen West-Knights
articles.description: Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu . You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto , the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal? Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run. articles.title: Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago | Kayode Akintola
articles.description: The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease . That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying . There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths . The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
articles.description: When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement? What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.” Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers

As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong. The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species. articles.title: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape
articles.description: Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said. In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”. A few thousand short of capacity the stadium may have been, but 66,000 rocked it as of yore. Alas, Wales’s young side could not quite respond. This was a reversal of last weekend. It is not really worth dwelling on the fact that the second Leeds goal, a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty converted early in an astonishingly one-sided second half, came after Morgan Rogers was harshly penalised for handball. Leeds, superbly coached by Daniel Farke and up to sixth after two clinical strikes from Noah Okafor, Calvert-Lewin’s sixth goal of the season and a late effort from Brenden Aaronson, were so dominant that they had no real need for a helping hand from the officials. Sabah Kerjota and Pierre Landry Kaboré both scored twice with Claudio Braga, Sabri Guendouz, Stuart Findlay and a Ryan Finnigan own goal completing the rout. Vrancken was naturally delighted that his players had ended a run of three defeats in a row in such spectacular style. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson
articles.description: Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation. Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I didn’t know’: former Australia Test coach Darren Lehmann denies any knowledge of sandpaper use
articles.description: Lehmann’s version of events of 2018 tour remain unchanged ‘We’ve just got to try to move on’ from ball tampering saga Darren Lehmann has denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper to alter the ball during Australia’s Test tour of South Africa in 2018, contradicting Cameron Bancroft’s claims. The former Australian Test coach was implicated in Bancroft’s 4,000-plus word statement on the events that led to the Western Australian being busted on-field with sandpaper down his trousers in Cape Town. Continue reading...
